1:
Wesley opens by correcting the English: the offering is of meal, not meat, the familiar rendering being an old misprint that has run through many editions. How many kinds the chapter describes is not agreed: Clarke counts five — plain flour, cakes and wafers from the oven, cakes from the pan, cakes from the frying-pan, and parched green ears — while Ellicott counts three, treating the baked sorts as one class. Gill notes that the Hebrew says when a soul, which the Targum turns into a man, and reports the Jewish comment that the word suits a freewill offering made with the whole heart, as though the offerer presented his own soul; he runs through the derivations proposed for the name, from bringing, from delighting, or from a Chaldee word for a gift. Ellicott adds that the flour was wheat and worth double the ordinary barley, and that it was kept among the Temple stores. Henry and Wesley agree on why such an offering was appointed, that it stooped to the poor, so men living on bread and cakes could bring their own homely fare, and that God accepts the meanest service sincerely meant; Henry recalls that the first offering named in scripture was of this kind, and compares the little cake made first for the prophet at Sarepta.

The oil and the frankincense are explained two ways, and the difference is characteristic. Ellicott gives practical reasons: oil was to that table what butter is to ours, added to make the portion palatable to the priests who would eat it, and the frankincense was there to counteract the smell of flesh burnt on the altar. Wesley takes the oil for the graces of the Spirit. Calvin faces the question behind both, granting that God is drawn neither by sweetness of taste nor by pleasant scents, and holding that such symbols were useful for teaching a rude people lest they corrupt his service with inventions of their own; from the same principle comes the rule the chapter runs on, that nothing impure be offered, the flour sifted fine so the oblation should not be defiled with bran. Clarke supplies a control that supports the practical reading, noting that neither oil nor incense went with the sin offering or the offering of jealousy, because those were not offerings of memorial but brought iniquity to remembrance.

Whom the memorial reminds is the neatest disagreement here. Clarke says it put God in mind of his covenant with their fathers; Ellicott says it brought the worshipper into the grateful remembrance of God and reminded him of the promise to accept, citing the psalm that asks the Lord to remember all thine offerings and the word to Cornelius that his prayers had come up for a memorial; Wesley allows both, that the offerer is reminded the whole is God's and that God, to speak after the manner of men, is put in mind of his promises. On what was burnt and what kept, Clarke observes that a handful only went to the fire while the rest was reserved for the priest, but all the frankincense was burnt, since from that the priest could draw no advantage. Ellicott sets the offering in its class, among the most holy rather than the less holy, so that it might be eaten only by the priests and only in the court. Gill draws two conclusions from the same provision, that it shows the care taken for the priests' maintenance, from which the apostle argues for the support of ministers, and that those made priests by Christ may feed on him. Calvin makes the delivery into the priest's hand the point, private persons being shut out of that honour so the peculiar dignity of Christ should stand; Keil describes the oven, which was no baker's oven but a large pot of the kind still used in the East.
4:
The three vessels are identified by comparison with what is still used in the same countries. Ellicott makes the first a portable pot about three feet high and open at the top, easily broken, into whose heated sides the thin oval dough is thrown so that it bakes in minutes, coming out soft enough to roll like paper and hardening as it stands. Clarke prefers an etymology, deriving the name from a root meaning to split, on account of the dissolving heat. Wesley says only that it was made in the sanctuary for the purpose, and Gill adds the rule that a man who vowed an offering of this kind could not discharge the vow with one baked otherwise. For the second vessel Clarke gives a flat iron plate over the fire, what some countries call a griddle; Keil agrees it was iron and large and flat, and traces its survival among the Arabs, the Turcomans of Syria and the Armenians, noting that the Berbers and Kabyles use a shallow iron pan whose name is the very word the Greek translators chose here. Ellicott would render it a flat plate and describes the convex fire-plate set on stones about nine inches from the ground with the fire beneath, adding that the baking was done in the court where the vessels of ministration were kept.

Over the third they divide, and the disagreement is worth marking because it is about the same Arabic word. Clarke identifies it with the shallow earthen vessel called a ta-jen, used for frying and much else, and supports it out of the travellers who describe how bread is baked in Barbary, either directly on the coals or in such a dish. Keil and Ellicott both refuse that. Keil denies the gridiron the Greek version supplies and argues from the root, which means to boil, that a vessel for boiling must be meant, so that these were cakes boiled in oil; Ellicott renders it boiled in a pan and describes something deeper, nearer a stew-pan than a frying-pan. The difficulty is that Keil has already given the ta-jen as the Greek rendering of the second vessel, not the third, so the two accounts assign the same foreign word to different pans. Gill settles the distinction from the Jewish authorities rather than from travellers: the deeper vessel has a lip and the paste in it runs thin, while the shallower has none and its paste is stiff enough not to spread.

On the breaking up of the cake there is more agreement. Gill takes it as answering to the dividing of the burnt offering and reports the rule that everything prepared in a vessel had to be cut, one cake folded into two and two into four, each piece about the bulk of an olive. Ellicott notes that bread broken and steeped in oil is a dish still in favour among the Bedouin. Keil observes that the pieces were to be broken for the offering and the oil poured over them. Gill alone reads the whole series of operations as a figure, taking the mixing and kneading, the baking and frying, the cutting in pieces and the burning of part on the altar to signify the sufferings by which Christ was made at once an atonement for sin and food for faith.
8:
Clarke thinks the offerer brought the prepared cake to the priest himself, who then presented it before the Lord. Ellicott fills in the later procedure: whichever of the three preparations was chosen, the pieces were put into a ministering vessel, the oil and frankincense added to them there, the vessel carried by the offerer as far as the priest, and by the priest to the south-west corner of the altar. Keil observes that presenting an offering made of these things — the several kinds of pastry just described — was in the main the same as presenting the plain flour at the chapter's opening. Gill specifies the handful taken for the memorial: as of the fine flour, so of the pieces baked in the oven, the pan, or the fryingpan. What was left, he notes, was simply what had not been burnt with fire, and it fell to Aaron and his sons as a thing most holy.

On the ban that follows, the witnesses agree about leaven and divide about honey. Henry refers the first to the unleavened bread of the exodus, the offerings requiring too much despatch to wait for leavening, and reads the later comparison two ways: leaven swells, as pride and hypocrisy do, and it sours, as malice does. Wesley adds that the prohibition binds the freewill offering, leaven being permitted in others. Calvin makes the rule general — that God's service is corrupted if any strange invention is mingled with it, which is what Christ meant by the leaven of the Pharisees — and Gill supplies the rabbinic safeguard that meat offerings were kneaded in hot water so that they should not leaven at all. Honey is the harder case. Ellicott disposes of it in a line, that honey was anciently used to produce fermentation and is therefore excluded like fermented dough; Clarke suspects rather that it gripes and purges, and remarks that the College of Physicians had on that account left it out of all medicinal preparations. Calvin canvasses the guesses of others — sweet fruits, the impurity of the bee, an offensive smell in burning, the practice of the Gentiles — and prefers his own, that cooked honey turns sour and ferments the bread it is mixed with. Both are allowed back at the firstfruits: Gill cites the Targum, that leavened bread and dates were offered then, and Wesley marks the limit, that they might be offered but not burnt, being reserved for the priests.

Salt is required where leaven is refused, and Clarke sets the two against each other: salt preserves from putrefaction and so stands for the purity and persevering fidelity the worship of God demands, and the covenant is called a covenant of salt because salt is incorruptible. He notes that the heathen used it as freely, no sacrifice being offered without the salted meal, and gives most of a page to Pliny's chapter on it, down to the derivation of the soldier's salary. Ellicott takes the same qualities in a social direction: salt is the token of hospitality and friendship in the East, the Arabs sealing a compact by laying it on a sword-blade and each taking a little into his mouth, and to be salted with the salt of the palace is to be bound in fidelity to the king. Wesley holds both senses together, incorruption of mind and the perpetuity of the covenant, adding that to neglect the salt was itself a breach of covenant. Calvin turns it inward: no worship has savour except what is seasoned by God's word, and the saying that every one shall be salted with fire means that believers must endure to be refined. Henry says the sacrifices were in themselves unsavoury and all religious service must be seasoned with grace; Gill hears in it Christ, savoury food to his people and to the Father alike.
14:
The last kind is of firstfruits, and Ellicott would move the paragraph: these three verses belong immediately after the exception granted for leaven and honey, the intervening verse on salt being a general remark that closes the directions for all the bloodless offerings, and such transpositions are not uncommon in the Hebrew scriptures. Whether the offering was owed or volunteered is disputed. Calvin distinguishes it sharply from the firstfruits proper, which were paid in obedience to the law, this being an addition a man might make of his own out of his new corn. Wesley says the same in fewer words, that these are firstfruits of one's own freewill, there being others whose time, quality and proportion God had appointed. Gill reports the Jewish authorities on both sides: Aben Ezra takes it for a voluntary offering and not one of those required at the passover, at pentecost or at tabernacles, while Jarchi and Gersom refer it to the offering of the Omer, brought on the sixteenth of Nisan, which Gill says is the general sense of the Jewish writers.

On the material the witnesses are unusually concrete. Keil parses the two Hebrew terms: the first names ears parched or roasted at the fire, the second something rubbed to pieces, from a root meaning to rub, and the word he renders field-fruit is elsewhere a corn-field, or in the prophets cultivated ground as against desert, used here for what the ground bears. Calvin thinks the two phrases describe one thing rather than two, the ears being dried at the fire so that they might be pounded the more easily and then burnt with the oil and frankincense; he presses the word full, so that the people should choose good ears and bring nothing poor or stunted. Clarke and Ellicott both observe that this is ordinary food and not a ceremonial curiosity: green or half-ripe wheat parched with fire is still eaten by the poor of Palestine and Egypt, Clarke says, and Ellicott that parched corn was and remains a favourite article of diet in the East and was therefore a fit offering, governed by the same rules as the other two kinds.

The handling is the same as before. Gill notes that the oil and the frankincense were laid either on the dried ears or on the flour once they had been ground, exactly as on the wheaten flour and on the cakes and wafers earlier, and that the memorial burnt was a portion of the beaten corn, or of what had been ground in a mill, with part of the oil and all of the frankincense. Clarke draws the picture out: because the tabernacle was God's house, with its golden table and its bread, he is represented as keeping a table among his people and partaking of the same food they live on, sitting down with the poor to a meal of parched corn; and Clarke reads the offering as a thanksgiving for seed time and for the prospect of harvest. Wesley ends on the fire rather than on the grain, taking it for the fervency that ought to be in every religious service — holy love is the fire by which all our offerings must be made, and without it they are no sweet savour.
